en: Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the best of men, as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī and Vyāsa, one should then utter the word "Victory" at the beginning of the Bhīṣmaparvan.
When the kings had assembled at Kurukṣetra, that abode of merit, while the world remained within the range of the sun's rays, Bhmj_6.2.
When the armies had become one in the battle between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas, and when all directions—save for the old and the young—had been reduced to emptiness; Bhmj_6.3 //
When dreadful omens had appeared on all sides,
the two armies came within each other's range of vision, marked by their banners.
Hṛṣīkeśa and Dhanañjaya blew their conchs with great enthusiasm;
by the deep resonance of those two, the worlds trembled.
"Those in a disadvantageous position must not be slain, nor those who have withdrawn from the army,
nor those when the battle has ceased"— thus did the kings establish the code of conduct.
In the meantime, the lord of sages, the son of Parāśara, having approached,
spoke to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who was dejected and staying within his palace.
O King, in this entire assembly of heroic rulers of the earth,
a terrible destruction of the kṣatriyas has now arrived.
"Accept this divine eye and witness the battle yourself," when the sage had said this, the king, his heart agitated, replied:
"O Blessed One, I do not venture to behold the death of my kinsman;
yet, because that which is destined must inevitably come to pass, I am unable to prevent it."
When the king had spoken thus, the sage, the bestower of boons, having granted Sañjaya divine vision, addressed the monarch once more.
"Saṃjaya will relate this entire battle to you;
for one who possesses divine vision, there shall be nothing unknown to him."
O Dhṛtarāṣṭra, because of your misconduct, Death yawns toward the kings;
for ill omens are seen that whisper of total destruction.
Rohiṇī is severely afflicted by Saura, the quarters are ablaze,
births are abnormal, and the sun is shrouded by Kabandha.
The sky is filled with flesh-eating beasts, and the clouds rain down blood;
what else is there? Alas, the queen of kings—will the earth no longer exist?
The fire has its flames turning to the right, and likewise there is serenity of mind;
this manifestation of the signs of victory exists wherever Dharma is present.
Hundreds are conquered by one, yet one cannot be conquered even by hundreds;
for this edge of the sword is tremulous, and no certainty is to be found therein.
When the lord of sages had thus spoken and quickly vanished, the king questioned Saṃjaya regarding the configuration of the continents; and being thus questioned, he replied.
O King, within the vast, mirror-like orb of the cool-rayed moon,
the entire expansive continent of Sudarśana is reflected.

On this island, shaped like a jewel and surrounded by the salt ocean, there stands in the center a lofty mountain of gold, like the pericarp of a lotus; on one side it has the shade of the *pippala* tree, and on the other it has the shape of a hare. Bhmj_6.20.
Other mountain ranges,
beginning with Himālaya, stand upon the two sides of that central mountain like reclining serpents, reaching from the east to the west.
Himavat, Hemakūṭa, and Niṣadha are on the south;
on the north are Śṛṅgavat, Nīla, and Śveta—these are of great power. (Bhājana-loka 6.22)
Between these various jewel-adorned regions lie the lands of the continents;
the land of Bharata is the land of karma, while the others are lands of fruition.
In Harivarṣa and the other regions, there is a creation of beings resembling the god of love;
it is the abode of those who have performed meritorious deeds, where the place known as Gaṇḍikā is renowned.
Likewise, below Mount Meru lies Jambūkhaṇḍa; from the flow of its fruit is born the pure Jambū river, which produces gold known as jāmbunada.
Having drunk that very [river], the inhabitants of Uttarakuru are freed from death;
because of its name, this continent is called after it, reaching as far as heaven.
Having spoken thus, Sañjaya went to Kurukṣetra, onto the battlefield,
and having met with Dhṛtarāṣṭra, he reported the destruction of his own soldiers.

***** The Formation of Jambūkhaṇḍa // 1 // ***** Listen, O King: Śantanu’s son, having slain infinite vassal lords, brought about a state of uncertainty regarding victory for the sons of Pāṇḍu. (Bhājana-mañjarī 6.28)
In that field where the kṣatriyas were destroyed, at the assembly of all the kṣatriyas,
while Duryodhana was exceedingly enraged and possessed great pride in his vast army—
When the ocean of forces was stirred up by the sound of the conch of Gāṅgeya,
it was followed by the sound of the conchs of the Pārthas, led by the *pāñcajanya*.
When the expanse of the world was filled and the quarters seemed to tremble with its thunderous roar,
the glorious Vijaya— the refuge of all armies and whose charioteer was Acyuta— [advanced].
He beheld the teachers, relatives, and kinsmen among the Kuru armies;
considering that they were acting like moths in the fire of his own majesty,
the sorrowful treasury of compassion spoke to Govinda.
"Alas! For the sake of a mere fragment of a kingdom, O Kṛṣṇa, this effort of ours—so deluded—is filled with such fury even over the slaughter of our own kinsmen."
Having descended from the noble lineage established by the sequence of praise for virtuous conduct,
how could one such as I enjoy a fortune that must be attained through the murder of a guru?
Having spoken thus, Bībhatsu, his eyes filled with tears, out of compassion dropped the Gāṇḍīva from his hand upon the chariot and sat down in despondency.

***** The First Chapter of the Śrīmadbhagavadgītā ***** Seeing him overcome by grief, Madhusūdana said: "Why this despondency from you, who possess the essence of fortitude, at such an untimely moment? (BhG 2.1)
O Pārtha, you are a spirited and proud kṣatriya who would purchase glory even at the cost of your life; you ought not to abandon your own family tradition, which is consistent with dharma.
Whether joined or separated from the body,
what person of true wisdom would grieve for the embodied soul within this manifold expansion of universal illusion?
Just as the states of pleasure and so forth belong to the body at various times according to their respective kinds,
so too do the bodies belong to this embodied being who exists, yet is devoid of substantial existence.
For one who endures the perishable unions of sense objects and senses— which bring about joy and sorrow— having relinquished the self, for him there is eternal nirvāṇa.
For this unborn, ancient, and imperishable embodied self,
this assumption of a body is like the shedding and replacement of withered leaves.
In its beginning, middle, and end, this embodied being—whose nature consists of both the manifest and the unmanifest—is always existent; for it never ceases to be.
Casting aside the shrinking from infamy, you who possess a vast resolve,
enter the battle with your mind set upon heaven, regarding victory and defeat as equal.
Relying on the intellect of yoga, free from the bondage of karma,
enjoy that state which transcends the qualities (guṇas) and is devoid of the ritual acts of the dry Vedas.
For the learned in all the Vedas, this alone is the purpose,
just as it is for those who fetch water when reservoirs are full.
Free from attachment and renouncing the fruits [of action], perform your duties ever with a disciplined mind;
for trade is indeed for those who seek rewards, but you must serve only the Supreme Lord.
When your intellect, freed from delusion, shall attain tranquility,
you will then be fulfilled, having no further regard for the matters you have heard.
Thus addressed by Pārtha, who had asked for the characteristics of one whose wisdom is steady and who is absorbed in samādhi, the Blessed One spoke as follows.
Realizing "I am not other than the Lord," filled with his own bliss and having cast aside all volitional thoughts, he is called one whose wisdom is firmly established.
He who dwells restraining his limbs like a tortoise and refraining from desires,
whose intellect is steady due to the absence of contemplation on sense-objects— he does not perish.
Even through arduous austerities, the sense objects wither away like sapless wood for those who are indifferent and dispassionate, constantly perceiving the inner self.
He who remains awake during times when others are overcome by sleep and when the darkness of ignorance prevails,
attains the state of Brahmā, as unshakeable as the great ocean.
***** The Second Chapter of the Śrī Gītā ***** Having heard this, Arjuna, his mind agitated, said to Kṛṣṇa: "How is it that, speaking thus, you urge me into this terrible battle? (BhG 2.54)
O Lord, although you have stated that wisdom is superior to action,
you yourself praise me— who am fit only for the dull-wittedness of action— thereby deluding me.
When Śvetāśva said, "Speak what is better," Keśava replied:
"I have declared that the final goal consists of both knowledge and action, pertaining to Sāṃkhya and Yoga."
A person is not liberated from action by merely refraining from undertaking it nor by its renunciation;
for his senses, such as hearing and the rest, continue to run forcefully toward their respective objects.

Even when their organs of action are restrained, those performers of ritual acts who are attached to false conduct and whose inner states are fixed, remember everything with their minds. (Bhājana-vastu 6.58)
For action is indeed better than inaction, since sacrifice cannot exist without action;
those who consume only the remnants of sacrifice are like virtuous trees, whereas those who enjoy only for themselves are mere consumers.
When a person, though engaged in action, becomes free from attachment and remains content in the state of delighting in the Self, then he desists from activity.
"In former times, Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone;
therefore, do not turn away from what must be done, so that the world may follow your example."
This task is also for me, who have fulfilled my purpose and am intent on protecting the established order;
otherwise, the world would perish, unrestrained by my authority.
An ordinary person is not a worthy vessel for those who are fit for omniscience;
therefore, one should not encourage them, like trying to urge on lame men who are already moving with speed.
Fight, having surrendered all actions to me and remaining free from anxiety; for those who always abide by my teaching cross over the terrible darkness.
Abandoning passion and hatred, which arise from what is pleasant and unpleasant, perform everything that is appropriate for your nature, remaining devoted to your own duty.
Having heard this, Arjuna said: "Impelled by whom does a powerless living being commit sin, as if forcibly brought under control?"
Thus questioned, Hṛṣīkeśa, the Lord of the worlds,
spoke [to him who was] possessed by the quality of passion (rajas), which gives rise to joy, sorrow, and the like.
By this powerful and terrible enemy, which is characterized by the destruction of the world, which is kin to desire and a relative of anger, and which is the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
The soul is obscured by impurity, just as water is covered by duckweed, the pure sky by dust, or the risen sun by a cloud. (Bhājana-vastu 6.69)
O you who can take any form at will, destroy that unbearable enemy who is joined with mind and intellect, whose abode is the cage of the senses. Bhmj 6.70.

***** The Third Chapter of the Śrī Gītā ***** This yoga, which was obtained by Manu from me in former times through the Sun, and which had been lost over time, has now been declared by me to you. Bhmj_6.71 //
"You are a witness to many births, my devoted companion;
yet your former body has not come within the range of my memory."
But I, for the sake of the stability and protection of the virtuous,
appear age after age for the destruction of those who are evil-minded.
This action does not bind me, for I am the performer of dharma who has not [previously] committed [unrighteousness].
You too, being unattached and free from desire, perform the duty appropriate to your lineage.
The distinction between action, inaction, and mis-action is difficult to discern,
due to their divisions into that which is appropriate for oneself, that which is devoid of fruit, and that which is contrary.
He who perceives the state of actionlessness through the renunciation of the fruits of action,
and who understands that action arises from the absence of [egoistic] action out of fear of sin— he is wise.
One whose karma has been burnt by the fire of knowledge, who is eternal bliss, independent,
free from desire, and devoid of egoism— such a sacrificer merges into Brahman.
Having offered the oblation consisting of Brahman into the fire of Brahman by means of the offering of Brahman,
one who is devoted to the sacrifice of the vital breaths proceeds to Brahman through meditative absorption in Brahman.
Having offered the senses into the fire of self-restraint, the objects of the senses into the fire of the senses,
and the actions of those [senses] into the fire of the yoga of the Self, they go to the supreme goal.
Even those who sacrifice with material austerity, yoga, recitation, and knowledge,
having here restrained the prāṇa and apāna breaths within the channels, perform concentration (dhāraṇā).
Those who are free from stain surrender their entire knowledge;
consuming the nectar that remains from sacrifice, they go to the supreme abode.
By serving such wise ones with prostrations,
they will effortlessly cause you to perceive the All-Seer within your own self.
"Purified by the fire of knowledge, you shall become pure;
for those who possess faith, knowledge manifests of its own accord in the course of time."
The deluded who indulge in doubt perish, but not those whose doubts have been dispelled. Since the wise remain free from doubt, arise for the sake of spiritual prosperity.
***** The Fourth Chapter of the Śrī Gītā ***** Having heard that, Pārtha again questioned Madhusūdana:
"O Janārdana, tell me which is superior: renunciation or the yoga of action? (BhG 5.1)
Thus questioned, Śauri replied: "Both of these lead to liberation;
however, it is my conviction that the yoga of action is superior to renunciation."
Even while hearing, speaking, touching, and even while attached to their own activities,
they do not cling, like the rays of the sun upon the mud.
That very same thing is prescribed as the slight merit or demerit of men;
yet when knowledge is obscured by ignorance, what indeed is this latent impression of karma?
Those possessed of knowledge, having dispelled [ignorance] through knowledge, have attained the supreme consummation;
whether toward a Brahmin or a dog-cooker, these wise ones possess equal vision.
For those who are dispassionate toward external pleasure— which is subject to suffering and perishable—
the supreme light becomes clear through their delight in internal bliss.
Having cast aside external sensations, with the gaze fixed between the eyebrows and holding the prāṇa and apāna breaths equally within the nose, one should strive for liberation.
Free from sensual desire, intoxication, hatred, fear, and anger,
and devoid of egoism and the darkness of ignorance, one who is without envy finds peace.

***** The Fifth Chapter of the Glorious Gītā ***** He who performs his own duty with action, free from desire for fruit, having transcended the stage of one desiring to ascend, is established in yoga and is devoid of envy. (6.93)
Immovable and satisfied with knowledge, he perceives the Self by means of the self;
seated in equanimity and possessing a tranquil form, he is like an ocean without waves.
One who beholds the tip of the nose, whose self is tranquil, approaches me through meditative concentration—
provided that his activities such as eating are regulated and his mind is ever unshakable.
The attainment of the Self indeed occurs for the yogi who has abandoned desire;
by restraining the mind, they perceive that [Self], from whatever [sense-object] it might otherwise flow away.
One should perceive oneself, me, and everything everywhere within my self;
for this flickering mind, restraint is achieved only through dispassion.
"By such powerful practice, it is like a turbulent wind.
Having heard this, the son of Kuntī questioned Keśava again.
"O Lord, what is the fate of one who has fallen from yoga due to the fickleness of the mind?
Being thus questioned again by Arjuna, the Blessed One replied:
Even a person who has fallen from yoga will become a doer of good;
having enjoyed divine happiness for a long time, he will be preceded by auspiciousness.
Whether among the enjoyers of worldly pleasures or among yogis, one born into a family of great beings recovers through subsequent births that which was practiced in former lives;
therefore, O Arjuna, become a yogi whose yoga is superior in austerity and knowledge.
***** The Sixth Chapter of the Śrī Gītā ***** With his mind perpetually fixed upon me, a person knows me through devotion;
I am the eightfold-formed one, the soul of all that is moving and unmoving. (6.102)
The wise know me to be the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction;
all beings are animated by me, and everything is established in me.
Deluded, he does not recognize me as bearing the goddess Māyā;
but those who know me as Māyā are always successful.
One who seeks wealth, one who desires knowledge, one who is distressed, or a man of wisdom—anyone may take refuge in me;
yet I am eternally dear to the wise man, for I am within the range of his vision.
Devoted to no other deity, full of faith and free from doubt, those seeking liberation worship me, [thinking]: "Vāsudeva is everything."
They know me as that which is called Brahman, the inner self, and action, together with the elemental beings,
the presiding deities, and the sacrifice— even at the dissolution of the body.
When "Acyuta" had been spoken, the son of Śakra addressed him:
"O Blessed One, what is this Brahman? What is said to be the Adhiyajña? (BhG 7.1)
Thus questioned, Hṛṣīkeśa spoke to Śvetavāhana:
"The imperishable Supreme Brahman is the state of being; such is the Adhyātma of the Self."
Free from attachment, one performs the action that creates existence; sovereignty over transient things is the presiding deity (adhibhūta).
I alone am the presiding divinity (adhidaiva) here, for I, the all-pervading Lord, am also the presiding sacrifice (adhiyajña).
Those who, at the time of death, remember me with a cultivated mind, truly enter into me;
for the final state of beings corresponds to their mental disposition at the end of life.
Those who constantly remember the ancient poet, the teacher more subtle than even the subtle, who is beyond darkness and possesses the radiance of the sun; Bhmj_6.112 //
Those who have fixed their vital breaths between the eyebrows, piercing the aperture of Brahmā and chanting the single-syllabled Brahman "Om," go to the Supreme.
The creation of beings by Brahmā and the others revolves like a wheel; yet those who have attained Me, the Supreme, do not come into existence again in this world.
In this Vairañca [cycle], during the day and night, beings come into existence and cease to exist;
yet the one Blessed One, the unmanifest, does not perish.
The day is full of splendor and white; it is the northern course (uttarāyaṇa) solely for the sake of liberation.
***** The Eighth Chapter of the Glorious Gītā ***** Listen, O Phalguna, to this other secret of kings, which is sacred;
one who lacks faith and is enslaved by the cycle of rebirth does not attain Me. (Bhagavadgītā 6.116)
All beings exist within me, the creator of all, but I do not exist within them;
the worlds abide in me and yet do not abide in me, like winds in the sky.
This primordial nature, presided over by me, gives birth to the moving and the unmoving;
yet those whose vision is clouded by impurity do not know me, for I am unattached.
Those of virtuous deeds know me as the sacrifice that pervades all, the object of knowledge, the seed of existence and non-existence, and the cause of all causes. (Bhagavadgītā 6.119)
Those who follow the dharma of the three Vedas, being distressed by the perishability of attaining enjoyments in heaven,
do not reach me, as they are bound by the fetters of dry ritual action.
Those who have acted rightly, who always take refuge in him alone and worship no other,
come of their own accord to his state, even if they are born from another womb.
***** The Ninth Chapter of the Glorious Gītā ***** Listen once more with affection, my friend, for you are being instructed:
even the hosts of immortals and the sages do not know Me in truth. (BhG 6.122)
Whatever excellent and prosperous thing you see in this world of moving and unmoving beings, that is I, the self of all beings; for nothing exists apart from me.
I am Viṣṇu, I am Sūrya, I am Candra, I am Maghavan;
I am Śaṅkara, I am Dhaneśa, as well as Vahni and the Preceptor of the Gods; I am the Imperishable, I am Time, I am Victory, and I am also Prosperity.
***** The Tenth Chapter of the Śrī Gītā ***** Having heard this, Pārtha said: "I know you, O Acyuta, in every way;
yet, O All-pervading Lord, I desire to see Your form composed of the entire universe. (BhG 11.1)
Thus addressed by the son of Pāṇḍu, the Blessed One, the slayer of Kaiṭabha,
revealed his universal form through the power that manifests the universe.
Within the body of that abode of the universe, which possessed infinite heads, eyes, and thousands of arms,
the entire world was seen dissolved.
Seeing the sky filled with a splendor whose brilliance surpassed that of the sun and fire, Pārtha, his hair standing on end, spoke to him with palms joined in reverence: Bhājana-vyūha 6.128.
I behold you, whose vast body is pervaded by the host of exalted gods,
and by which [body] of uninterrupted extent everything has been filled.
I do not venture to behold that very body, which is without end or limit and crowded with Brahmā, Rudra, the Maruts, Agni, the lords of sages, and serpents.
I see those heroes headed by Bhīṣma and Droṇa having entered your mouths,
which are formidable with tusks, like the mouths of Time at the end of an eon.
Who are you, O destroyer, with a body so fierce that it brings about the destruction of all things,
who have yourself prepared to burn the entire world without cause?
When the son of Kuntī had spoken thus, Madhusūdana said:
"I am the destroyer of kings, consecrated for the task of uprooting and destroying the world."
Having slain those heroes who were at the forefront of Kuru’s army and who were previously destroyed by me,
may you attain the fame and prosperity appropriate to your lineage.
Having heard those words of the enemy of Kāliya, Pārtha, with palms joined in reverence,
spoke with a trembling mind, bowing down with a faltering voice.
The worlds rejoice at your fame when it is praised by the Siddhas and Cāraṇas;
the Rākṣasas flee from your radiance; this is fitting for you, O Janārdana. (Bhājana 6.136)
I bow again and again to You— the abode of the world, whose form is the universe, who transcends the senses, the infinite and eternal light, the Self of all.

"Forgive that [which was said] by me in the past when, O Kṛṣṇa, O Govinda, you were addressed by me as 'Yādava'— you who are yourself dear to those who bow before you, and who were spoken to thus by your friend."
"O Blessed One, having thus seen that great and formidable form,
I see the entire world in its totality as if mounted upon a wheel."
Be gracious, O Lord, and show me that very same gentle form;
my mind, distressed by this change, finds peace only suddenly through that [vision] and not otherwise.
Thus entreated by the bowing Kirīṭin, Kṛṣṇa then revealed his own four-armed form, just as it was.
"Even the gods do not see this all-pervading form of mine," having said this, the Lord of Kamalā consoled the son of Kuntī.

***** The Eleventh Chapter of the Śrī Gītā ***** Then Arjuna said to Kṛṣṇa: "Between those devotees who worship You as the unmanifest and imperishable, and those [who worship You as the manifest], which of them are more proficient in yoga? (BhG 6.143)
Thus questioned by Pārtha, Hari, having bestowed his grace, said:
"My devotees, endowed with faith, are in every way superior to the practitioners of yoga."
The attainment of me occurs through affliction alone by serving the unmanifest syllable;
even by those who know reality, the subtle and gross course is attained with difficulty.
My devotees attain the supreme state very quickly;
therefore, always keep your mind fixed on me and remain devoted to no other.
If your mind is not under control through practice, then seize it by force; if you are unable even in that, perform my work and constantly strive for your own welfare.
Alternatively, being devoted to Me, perform the renunciation of the fruits of actions;
for knowledge arises from supreme practice, and in this world, meditation is superior to knowledge.
From meditation comes the renunciation of fruits; therefore, peace is distinguished as superior.
One who is free from hatred, an ocean of compassion, equal in pleasure and pain, is tranquil. (Bhājana-vākya 6.149)
One who is impartial, pure, skillful, forgiving, and devoted is dear to me.
[Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the Śrī Gītā.
The wise say that the body is the field (kṣetra), and they know me to be the knower of the field (kṣetrajña).
But that field, along with its modifications, consists of Māyā and the elements beginning with Bhūta.
For those who are peaceful, who have seen the faults [of worldly life], and who possess knowledge, there is no delusion;
they abandon pride, hypocrisy, intoxication, and anger, and attend upon their guru.
There is constant non-attachment to that which is impermanent; knowledge is [the realization of this], while ignorance is otherwise.
That which is to be known is Brahman, consisting of the Self (manmaya), pure, and beyond both being and non-being. (Bhājana-vākya 6.152)
With hands and faces on all sides, possessing every form and free from ailment;
primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa)—this is the union of the field (kṣetra) and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña).
Prakṛti is the cause in the act of creation, while the Puruṣa is traditionally known as the enjoyer;
he who perceives the distinct nature of beings, even though they occupy a single location.
And through union with that, he attains the expansion of eternal Brahman.
This Supreme Self, transcending the qualities (guṇas), is imperishable due to its permanence;
though situated even within a physical body, it is all-pervading and remains unstained.
***** The Thirteenth Chapter of the Śrī Gītā-s ***** Listen further to this all-encompassing knowledge, served by the gods,
wherein Yoga arises within this womb of Brahman as the manifestation of form. (Bhājana-mālā 6.156)
These three qualities—sattva and the others—arise from that [unmanifest] and shine forth;
because of their constant diversity, embodied beings transmigrate.
Sattva is to be known as illuminating; rajas is that which causes agitation when it arises;
and tamas is indeed obscuring, from which delusion, negligence, and so forth originate.
Due to the constant mixture of these [qualities] and their variations in degree,
various virtues and defects are indeed observed among embodied beings.
My devotees, with peaceful minds, having attained the state of liberation while living,
are freed from these qualities and enjoy inexhaustible happiness.
***** The Fourteenth Chapter of the Śrī Kītāsūtra ***** The banyan tree of worldly existence has its roots above and extends upward as far as the abode of Brahmā;
it possesses many branches in the various worlds and has the diverse objects of the senses as its sprouts. (Bhājana-vastu 6.161)
He who knows that the arising of the fruits of good and evil for those awakened to their qualities and actions is not obstructed within the ground of their own nature— he is a knower of the Veda.
Having severed [the bonds] with the axe of non-attachment, they go to my state,
which is free from delusion, stainless, and surpassing the sun, the moon, and fire.
That portion which, as the all-pervading life-force, moves within this world of living beings,
departs taking with it the latent impressions of the senses, just as the wind carries away fragrance.
The wise perceive that supreme life-force of all worlds as being endowed with qualities in certain states, yet devoid of qualities in all conditions. Bhmj_6.165.
Having come as if to the creation of beings, I am the imperishable and eternal one;
those who possess fortitude, being absorbed in me, worship me, the Supreme Person.

***** The Fifteenth Chapter in the Śrī Gītā-s ***** Fearlessness, purity of being, knowledge, self-control, charity, austerity, sacrifice, non-violence, and other such qualities arise from those possessed of divine fortune. (Bhājya 6.167)
The demonic endowment is characterized by hypocrisy, pride, intoxication, anger, harshness, ignorance, and fickleness; it increases delusion and sorrow. (Bhagavadgītā 16.168)
"O friend, do not grieve even though you are constantly endowed with divine prosperity;
those who have fallen into an asuric state take on an asuric birth."
A person is known by their actions as being bound by qualities such as goodness (sattva) and the rest;
for the mental disposition, diet, and conduct of embodied beings are indeed equal to their inner qualities.

***** The Sixteenth Chapter of the Glorious Gītā ***** Having heard this, Phalguna then spoke again to Acyuta: "O Lord, I wish to know the true nature of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) and relinquishment (*tyāga*). (BhG 18.1)
When the son of Pāṇḍu had spoken thus, the Blessed One replied:
"The abandonment of the fruits of actions performed out of desire is what they declare to be renunciation."
The renunciation of the fruits of all actions is called "renunciation";
however, virtuous action is not to be abandoned, though that which is censured by the rules is to be abandoned.
The abandonment of obligatory duties out of delusion is said to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).
Abandonment due to the fear of afflictions and suffering is considered fruitless and of the nature of passion (rājasa).
The abandonment of those who act without attachment is regarded as being characterized by goodness (sāttvika).

Enraged by those hateful acts, Dhananjaya, whose charioteer was Hari and whose weapons were ablaze, wrought the destruction of the Kuru armies.

"O you who are blinded by intoxication, now that I am alive, where will you go?

Then, as the terrifying battle between Bhīṣma and Pārtha proceeded,
Virāṭa rushed toward Droṇa, the most eminent of all archers.
Droṇa, having covered that showerer of arrows with a rain of shafts,
let out a roar like the sound of a thundercloud and struck down his chariot.

As the lord of the Rākṣasas was roaring while fighting with illusory power,

While the kings who refused to retreat were being slain by Bhīṣma,

***** The Seventh Day of Battle // 28 // ***** When Bhīṣma had again formed the ocean array at dawn, the son of Drupada constructed the great Śṛṅgāṭaka array. Bhmj_6.365 //

Having slain the charioteer of the son of Śantanu with his arrows,

who were frantic with rut— as a lion slays elephants.

Having routed the Kaurava army, he roared, making the quarters of the sky resound;
like Rudra arisen for the destruction of all the worlds, he was accompanied by the gods.
Then the valiant Irāvān entered the Kuru army;
meanwhile, Ulūpī, the Nāga maiden, gave birth to Abhimanyu, the son of Phalguna.
Having been told by Arjuna in the city of the gods, "I myself shall provide assistance in this task," he went to that battlefield.
Carried by subterranean horses clad in armor of precious gold, he created,

Having gone there, he slew seven sons of Śakuni, warriors on horseback from Gāndhāra who led a vast army and possessed the prowess of clouds.

Then, resorting to a great illusion that deludes men,
those two of terrifying prowess entered the sky and fought.
As the Rākṣasa was being struck by Irāvat’s own floods of weapons,
a terrible roar arose, causing fear to all living beings.
Then the serpents, the offspring of the serpent-women, rendered assistance;

having devoured all the serpents, he resumed his own formidable body.
Then, while [the opponent] was bewildered by illusion, Arādirāva severed the head— adorned with earrings— from the body of the Rākṣasa with his sword.
When the son of Dhanañjaya was slain, the son of Hiḍimbā, overwhelmed with rage,

Seeing him rushing toward him, King Duryodhana himself,
together with all his own armies, fought that great master of illusion.
He slew the terrible night-stalkers who were followers of Hiḍimba— Vidyujjihva, Vegavān, Mahāraudra, and Pramāthin.
Then, before the eyes of the lord of the Vaṅgas, the king of the Kurus seized the spear hurled by Ghaṭotkaca with his great elephant.
When that Nāga had fallen and Suyodhana was protected,
the flesh-eater brought about the destruction of the enemy forces.
Then Bhagadatta, having put the army of the Pāṇḍavas to flight,
fought Ghaṭotkaca with his elephant Supratīka.
Having heard that his son had been slain, the son of Śatamanyu became enraged and made the earth impassable with the heads of the kings.
Bhīma also, consumed by rage now that his brother’s son had been struck down,
dispatched the heroic younger brothers of Suyodhana to the abode of Yama.
Anādhṛṣṭi, Kuṇḍalina, Kuṇḍabhedin, Sulocana,
Virāṭa, Dīrghabāhu, Subāhu, and Kanakadhvaja.
Having slain these Kauravas, he filled the army— crowded with hundreds of headless trunks—
with intoxicated *vetālas* at the close of day.
Then, when their bows and armor were cast aside and their chariots and elephants broken, those great car-warriors ordered the withdrawal of their armies from the battlefield.
***** On the eighth day of battle, the slaying of Irāvat.
****** Then, during the night, King Suyodhana, together with his younger brothers, summoned Karna and contemplated the defeat of the sons of Pṛthā. BhmJ_6.393.
The son of Vaikartana said to him, "Friend, let my word be done:
lay down your weapons against the son of Gaṅgā; I shall defeat the Pāṇḍavas."
This man is old and inactive, yet you have placed an excessive burden upon him— Dhananjaya— along with his allies, having done so entirely without reflection.
Having heard these words spoken by Karṇa, as if with hundreds of deeds performed out of joy,

With the quarters of space turned tawny by the rays of thousands of jewel-lamps,
and with its forests of luminous medicinal herbs blazing at night, it shone like a mountain inhabited by a multitude of beings.
Defeated by the radiance of his jeweled earrings, armlets, and crown,
the lamps before him became lusterless, as if overcome with shame.
He gazed upon the prostrate kings with feigned magnanimity,
as their names were announced by the circles of attendants according to their rank of valor.
With his necklace shimmering with its swaying motion,
he shone like the god of love with a foot-ornament that was a mass of nectar-waves from the moon.
Having reached the bright camp of the son of Śāntanu,
the illustrious one saw him lying upon a jeweled couch and prostrated before him.
Honored by the king and having accepted a seat,
Duryodhana reflected for a moment and then addressed his grandfather.
"This arm of yours, born of Bhrigu, which brings down the bow, is sufficient for the conquest of the three worlds; such is my opinion. (Bhājana-mañjarī 6.403)
If those Pāṇḍavas are to be protected out of compassion or kindness,
then give permission to Karṇa, who is fierce in battle, to fight.
Thus addressed by the Kuru king, as if struck in his vital organs, he said,
"You shall see [the result] at dawn," and sighing, he gazed upon the earth.
The Kaurava, too, having taken leave of him, returned to his own camp,

Then at dawn, when the Sarvatobhadra array had been formed by Bhīṣma together with Droṇa, the son of Droṇa, and others, standing at the head of the formation;
Amidst the counter-arrayed armies, the heroic Abhimanyu, along with the roaring sons of Pāṇḍu, tore through the front of the Kuru host.
Like the midday sun rising in the heat of summer, difficult to behold because of its hundreds of arrow-like rays,
the proud kings could not endure him, even when they were united.
Then Alambusa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, urged on by Duryodhana,
rushed toward him, wielding an illusion that deludes the three worlds.
By his great roar, which foretold the dissolution of the world,
many warriors suddenly fell, deprived of life.
Having engaged in battle for a moment with the sons of Draupadī who had arrived before him,

Then, with the splendor of the *arkāstra* weapon, the son of Subhadrā cut through that dark illusion (*tāmasī māyā*) produced by the rākṣasa who had split open the mountain with his arrows.
Then, in the battle, those led by Sātyaki, engaged with the followers of Droṇa’s son and the others,

Arjuna, approaching Droṇa— who was difficult to withstand due to his multitude of great weapons—

When the host of elephants was shattered by the blows of Bhīma’s formidable mace,
a river of blood flowed forth, garlanded with foam in the form of banners.
While that terrifying and chaotic battle was raging,
headless trunks were dancing to the rhythmic clapping provided by the *vetālas*.
Bhīṣma, difficult to endure with the flames of his broad arrows and having excellent warriors as his fuel,

Impelled by his arms, those arrows swiftly entered the kings like birds at evening entering trees thick with dense shade.
Like fireflies among trees, like locusts among rice stalks,

In that battle, Bhīṣma, bestowing his own glory as a poison upon the quarters, covered the directions with the severed chowries and turbans of the lords of the earth.
Having strewn the earth with the heads of kings, he, radiant with horripilation,
made it as if a pleasure-lotus pond for the Goddess of Battle.
The sparks of fire produced by the friction of helmets and arrows shone like the life-breaths of slain kings, now wandering as sky-dwellers through the air because of Bhīṣma.
Seized on all sides by the world with a dense net of arrows,
he created the illusion of a sudden night for all the armies.
When the Pāṇḍava army was torn asunder, with its armor shattered and the banners of its chariots cut down;
when the elephant divisions were broken and the kings were reduced to mere remnants.
When they had departed, casting aside their shame and discarding their bows, Keśava said to Arjuna, "Slay Bhīṣma in battle, for he is true to his promise."
Then Dhanañjaya, sighing with a dejected lotus-face and repeatedly censuring the duty of the Kṣatriyas, rushed toward his grandfather.
Seeing the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow risen up, raining down arrows,
as the army quickly rallied, the warriors fought once more.
Seeing Phalguna covered by arrows discharged from Bhīṣma’s bow,
the enemy of Kaṃsa abandoned his chariot and rushed toward him, using his arms as weapons.
Seeing that Kṛṣṇa had himself rushed forward in anger, Bhīṣma,
filled with a sense of blessedness and his form adorned with horripilation, spoke:
O Blessed One, I am the foremost among those who possess merit and the best among the accomplished,
since you, the Lord of the worlds, have yourself exerted yourself for my destruction.
When the son of Gaṅgā had spoken thus, Dhanañjaya quickly descended from his chariot and then led Kṛṣṇa back onto the vehicle.
Then, while the Kuru forest was strewn with the showers of Arjuna’s arrows,
the son of Śantanu once again brought about the destruction of the rulers of the earth.
In that terrible conflict, when the circle of great warriors had been broken,
the sons of Pāṇḍu withdrew at the end of the day.
***** The Ninth Day of Battle // 30 // ***** Then, in a secluded place, the King of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira), seeing the royal host broken by Bhīṣma, spoke sorrowfully to Janārdana: Bhmj_6.436 //
Behold, O Kṛṣṇa, by the awakened submarine fire of Gāṅgeya,

"Your task is not one that I may neglect; having now renounced my own time, I shall protect Bhīṣma in battle while the lords of the earth look on."

I do not see anyone in the worlds who could defeat me, a hero;

"My arrows do not fall upon one who is terrified by a weapon, nor upon one who was previously a woman;

Then at dawn, as the armies were arrayed in battle formations,

Śikhaṇḍin, shaking his bow with fierce anger, addressed him.
The son of Śāntanu said to him, "Strike at will, O son of Pṛṣata;

Approaching him as he was speaking thus, Śikhaṇḍin, his bow drawn into a circle, spoke to the son of the River with sighs of rage: Bhājya 6.451.
I know you to be of great power, even a conqueror of Bhārgava himself;

Having said this, the son of Pṛṣata covered him with a net of arrows,

Bhīṣma, disregarding him as well, pierced Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna with arrows and entered the Pāṇḍava army like a forest fire in a royal bamboo grove.
Then a fierce battle took place between the heroic and swift Kauravas and those led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna, as the faces of the quarters were shrouded in dust.
Then, by the command of Droṇa, the heroes headed by the son of Droṇa protected Bhīṣma in battle and fought against Dhanañjaya.
Then the son of Śāntanu, having utterly overwhelmed Virocana— whose crown was variegated with the rays of its jewels— with arrows possessing the weight of thunderbolts, [struck] the kings.

with a knitted brow, spoke from afar to Yudhiṣṭhira.

Then the heroes of the Kuru army, having surrounded the great chariot-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas for the protection of Bhīṣma, engaged in single combats.
Then, by the arrows of Gāṅgeya, even though they were released without effort,

Urged by Arjuna, Śikhaṇḍin drew his bow back to his ear and rushed toward him,
who possessed the power of the wielder of the broken-axe (Śiva).
Then, seeing the army urged on by Duryodhana himself while that slaughter of his own warriors was underway, the Grandfather [Bhīṣma]—
Having unleashed a terrible divine weapon, he rushed toward Dhanañjaya;
then, having reached the presence of Arjuna while Śikhaṇḍin stood before him.

then, when all his weapons had been severed by the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow—
In an instant, Bhīṣma became difficult to discern due to his arrows that left no gaps,

In that tumultuous and indistinguishable clash between the two armies during the afternoon,

The treasury of light fell, untouched by arrows,

The Grandfather, his own self unimpaired, attained his divine nature;
while the world was trembling, an incorporeal voice spoke: "Bhāj_6.481"

O Bhīṣma, being established in yoga, wait for the time of the northern course of the sun; O omniscient one, sustain your vital breaths within your heart, for you possess the power to determine the moment of your own death.
Having heard this supreme yoga, Suravrata attained it;
then, from the celestial host, [he received] that which was sent forth in the form of a swan.
Approaching him for that very purpose, the sages spoke to Bhīṣma;

Then Bhīṣma, gratified by that deed, praised Dhanañjaya and said to the Kaurava,

***** The Tenth Day of Battle // 31 // ***** Then,
when the night had passed and the kings were seated,

"But for the sake of Duryodhana, who honors his friends,
O father, grant me permission as I am prepared for battle."
Having spoken thus and being permitted by Bhīṣma,

Then the army of the bulls of the Kuru clan, eager for the King of Aṅga and whose pride and respect had been shattered by the vow of overcoming their enemies, reached a state of equality with the rushing forests shaken by the wind and water of the Sarayū.
